schools.summary: Augustine hears the Mediator himself, strong of hand in the conflict of the Passion, praying that the eternity of the Word may not be severed from that which as Man he is.

Calvin takes the psalm for David's usual practice after deliverance — the vows made in trouble first, then the thanksgivings — refers it to Saul's persecutions, and makes the comparison with the dead a measure of his straits: it is not enough to feel one's misery unless a man, renouncing all help from the world, betakes himself to God alone, which scarcely one in a hundred does; Gill hears in the cry a resolution to continue in prayer and direct it to the Lord only.

Henry hears a man afraid of a God angry at his prayers, asking both that God would speak to him with comfortable words and speak for him by pleading his cause, and says nothing can be so cutting to a gracious soul as the want of God's favour; Spurgeon makes the rock a resolve rather than a description, and holds that where formalists are content without answers, genuine suppliants need actual replies from heaven.

Clarke lays the psalm out in sections and refers it most probably to the captivity, will not confine the word rock to a metaphor of shelter but calls it also a fountain and the origin of all good possessed, and turns the verse into a charge against his own age's theology of unanswerable prayer.

Ellicott derives the Hebrew for rock from a root implying to bind together, so that the sense is strength and solidity rather than height, notes that the Septuagint suppresses the metaphor through timidity, prefers the Vulgate's 'be not silent from me', and thinks the pit suggests a bed of sickness; Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm in the persecution by Absalom.

debates.question: To what occasion does the psalm belong?

sides.position: most probably the captivity, though some give it to David
the persecution by Absalom, with the two preceding psalms

outliers.note: Reads the whole psalm as the voice of Christ, so that even the imprecation against enemies is not malevolence but the declaration of their punishment.

themes: them that go down into the pit

2.pericope_label: Hear my supplications; draw me not away with the wicked

schools.summary: Gill looks at what is lifted — supplications from the Spirit of grace, offered under a sense of unworthiness on the footing of mercy rather than merit — opens the plea three ways, and lists the works the wicked fail to regard: creation, providence, redemption and the Spirit's work on the soul, adding the Chaldee's reading that they do not understand the law of the Lord.

Spurgeon supplies the picture the verb wants, the wicked dragged off like felons drawn on a hurdle to Tyburn, and writes at length on those who speak peace with mischief in the heart — soft words oily with pretended love are the meshes of the infernal net, and it were better to be shut up in a pit with serpents than compelled to live with liars.

Clarke takes the oracle for the place in the holy of holies from which God answered the high priest, reads the imprecation as prediction rather than petition, and finds a prophecy literally fulfilled in Babylon, destroyed by Cyrus and never rebuilt; Wesley glosses the same holy of holies in a line and renders the plea 'drag me not'.

Ellicott prefers the margin, the shrine of thy sanctuary, would render the plea 'drag me not' after the vision in Ezekiel, and defends the imprecation as free of personal animosity, the poet being identified with devout Israel; Keil and Delitzsch mark the hinge of the psalm here, the first half praying and the second giving thanks.

debates.question: Is "give them according to their deeds" a prayer or a prophecy?

sides.position: prediction — the same as "thou wilt give them", a declaration of their lot
a petition, but one free of vindictiveness, praying that God vindicate himself

themes: lifting up the hands toward the oracle
draw me not away with the wicked
they speak peace but mischief is in their hearts
give them according to their deeds

6.pericope_label: Blessed be the Lord: my strength and my shield

schools.summary: Gill settles first what blessing God can mean — not invoking or conferring a blessing, neither of which a creature can do, but ascribing all blessedness to him — and takes the Lord for the author of both natural and spiritual strength, who would be the strength of David's heart in the hour of death.

Henry marks how soon the saints' sorrows are turned into songs, holds that what we win by prayer we must wear by praise, and finds a double benefit in trusting, since the very act of it helps a drooping spirit at a dead lift; Spurgeon calls prayer and praise the two lips of the soul and says real praise is no irrational emotion but rises like a pure spring from the deeps of experience.

Clarke reduces the confession to a persuasion that God hears, will answer and will save; Wesley explains why the help is spoken of as already had, God having assured David by his Spirit that the prayers were heard and accepted.

Ellicott finds the burst of thanksgiving discordant with the rhythm and sense of the rest, and reports the explanations offered — an interval before the writer resumed, two pieces joined, or an interpolation — and would render the rejoicing 'danceth for joy', noting that the Septuagint's 'my flesh has flourished' is probably the right reading of the last clause.

debates.question: Does the thanksgiving belong to the psalm as first written?

sides.position: no — it is discordant in rhythm and sense; an interval, a joining of two pieces, or an interpolation
yes — it is the same faith that prayed now giving thanks

themes: with my song will I praise him

8.pericope_label: The Lord is their strength: save thy people

schools.summary: Gill carries the pronoun back to the people already named, and observes the shape of the whole psalm, which begins with petitions for the psalmist and ends with prayers for the church — chosen, taken into covenant and given to the Son — so that this too is a prayer of faith.

Spurgeon calls the close a prayer for the church militant, written in short words but full of weighty meaning, insists we must pray for the whole church and not for ourselves alone, and finds a plea hidden in the words 'thy people'.

Clarke would emend the pronoun to 'to his people' on eight manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi with the versions behind them, notes that the Hebrew verb for feeding means also to govern, and sets the two eternities against each other — as hell is a bottomless pit, so heaven is an endless height in which there is eternal rising.

Ellicott reaches the same sense without the emendation, the people being throughout in the poet's thought even where the individual speaks, prefers 'stronghold of salvation' for the second phrase, and notes that the incorporation of this petition into the Te Deum links Christian worship with the Jewish.

debates.question: Should the text read "to them" or "to his people"?

sides.position: emend to "to his people" — eight manuscripts and the versions support it, and of its truth there can be no reasonable doubt
the received text already yields that sense, the people being throughout in the poet’s thought

themes: the saving strength of his anointed
save thy people, bless thine inheritance
feed them and lift them up for ever
